chapter_summary:
Firewalls are the first line of defense in network security, controlling traffic flow into and out of a system. While `iptables` has been the traditional Linux firewall, `nftables` is its modern successor, offering a more flexible, efficient, and easier-to-manage syntax. As an LFCE, mastering `nftables` is crucial for securing contemporary Linux environments. `nftables` uses a single framework for IPv4, IPv6, ARP, and bridge filtering, replacing the separate `iptables`, `ip6tables`, `arptables`, and `ebtables` utilities. Its core components are *tables*, *chains*, and *rules*. Tables (`nft add table ip filter`) define the address family (e.g., `ip`, `ip6`, `inet` for both), chains (`nft add chain ip filter input`) define the processing points (e.g., `input`, `forward`, `output`, `prerouting`, `postrouting`), and rules (`nft add rule ip filter input tcp dport 22 accept`) define the actions. The `inet` family is particularly useful as it allows you to write rules that apply to both IPv4 and IPv6 traffic without duplication.

One of the significant advantages of `nftables` is its ability to use *sets* and *maps*. Sets allow you to group multiple IP addresses, ports, or other match criteria into a single object, which can then be referenced in rules. This dramatically simplifies complex rule sets, improves performance, and makes management easier. For example, you can define a set of trusted IP addresses (`nft add set ip filter trusted_ips { type ipv4_addr; flags interval; }`) and then add multiple IPs to it (`nft add element ip filter trusted_ips { 192.168.1.0/24, 10.0.0.5 }`). A rule can then simply refer to this set: `nft add rule ip filter input ip saddr @trusted_ips accept`. Maps take this a step further, allowing you to map a match (e.g., an IP address) to a specific action or value (e.g., a port number). This is incredibly powerful for dynamic policies or load balancing. While `nftables` is powerful, remember that a misconfigured firewall can lock you out of your system. Always test new rules carefully, preferably in a test environment or with a console connection, and consider using `screen` or `tmux` sessions with a scheduled `at` job to revert changes if you get locked out (e.g., `echo "nft flush ruleset" | at now + 5 minutes`).

Network Address Translation (NAT) is another critical firewall function, particularly for servers acting as gateways or providing services to internal networks. `nftables` handles NAT with specific chains (e.g., `prerouting` for Destination NAT, `postrouting` for Source NAT) and the `snat` and `dnat` actions. For instance, to perform Source NAT (masquerading) for an internal network accessing the internet: `nft add table ip nat` then `nft add chain ip nat postrouting { type nat hook postrouting priority 100; }` and finally `nft add rule ip nat postrouting oifname "eth0" masquerade`. Destination NAT is used for port forwarding, allowing external traffic to reach internal services: `nft add rule ip nat prerouting iifname "eth0" tcp dport 80 dnat to 192.168.1.100:80`. Understanding the order of chain processing (hooks) and priorities is essential for correct NAT configuration. Common mistakes include forgetting to enable IP forwarding (`net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1` in `/etc/sysctl.conf`) or misconfiguring the interface names, leading to connectivity issues.

For environments still reliant on `iptables`, understanding its syntax and migration paths is important. `iptables` uses separate commands for IPv4 (`iptables`) and IPv6 (`ip6tables`), and its rules are organized into tables (`filter`, `nat`, `mangle`, `raw`) and chains (`INPUT`, `OUTPUT`, `FORWARD`, `PREROUTING`, `POSTROUTING`). A typical `iptables` rule might look like: `iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT`. Converting `iptables` rules to `nftables` can be done with the `iptables-restore-translate` utility, which helps in generating equivalent `nftables` rulesets. However, it's often better to re-architect the firewall directly in `nftables` to take advantage of its advanced features like sets and maps. Regardless of the firewall technology, preventing Denial of Service (DoS) attacks is a key concern. Firewalls can help by limiting connection rates (`limit` module in `iptables`, `limit rate` in `nftables`), blocking known malicious IP ranges, and dropping invalid packets. For example, `nft add rule ip filter input tcp dport 80 limit rate 10/second burst 20 packets drop` can help mitigate simple HTTP flood attacks. Always ensure your firewall rules are saved persistently (e.g., `nft list ruleset > /etc/nftables.conf` and enable `nftables.service` or `iptables-persistent` for `iptables`).

screens.title: Advanced Firewall Configuration with nftables/iptables
screens.subtitle: Practical, robust packet filtering, NAT, and migration strategies for modern Linux environments

narration.text: In this lesson you'll gain a practical grasp of modern Linux firewalling using nftables and the key points about legacy iptables. We'll begin by understanding the nftables architecture — tables, chains, and rules — and why the inet address family removes duplication between IPv4 and IPv6. You will see how sets and maps let you group IPs and ports for efficient rules, and how connection tracking enables stateful acceptance of returning traffic. We'll also cover NAT patterns: where to place SNAT and DNAT rules, how prerouting and postrouting hooks affect packet flow, and the essential step of enabling IP forwarding. Practical safety techniques will be emphasized, such as testing changes with a timed revert to avoid lockout. Finally, we'll discuss migrating iptables rules and when to translate versus re-architect in nftables. As you follow the hands-on scenario, you will practice allowing SSH, HTTP, and HTTPS; rate limiting SSH; creating a trusted internal set for management access; and performing destination NAT for port forwarding. Ready to build resilient rulesets that protect services without locking you out?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: nftables unifies packet filtering and NAT with flexible sets and maps, while safe testing and clear NAT rules keep services reachable and secure.

screens.title: nftables architecture: tables, chains, rules, and inet
screens.subtitle: How nftables organizes packet processing and why inet simplifies policy

narration.text: nftables structures packet filtering around three simple primitives: tables, chains, and rules. A table groups related chains and sets and is defined for a specific address family, such as ip, ip6, or inet. Chains are the processing points hooked into the kernel packet path — input, forward, output, prerouting, postrouting — and each chain has a type, hook, and priority that determine when it runs. Rules inside a chain define match conditions and actions, for example accepting TCP traffic to port 22. The inet family is a convenient abstraction that lets the same table hold both IPv4 and IPv6 rules. This removes the need to duplicate policies for IPv4 and IPv6 and reduces configuration drift. Concrete example: create an inet table, add an input chain with a default drop policy, and add an accept rule for ssh. A common misconception is that inet automatically handles protocol differences — it does not translate mismatched protocol semantics, but it does let you use a single ruleset for both families. Key takeaway: design tables by logical function, use chains to represent packet hooks, and prefer inet when managing dual-stack hosts to keep rules simpler and consistent. How might you split filtering responsibilities between tables and chains in a multi-role host?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Tables group chains by address family; chains represent hooks; rules match and act; inet covers both IPv4 and IPv6.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › nftables architecture
Concept: Tables, Chains, Rules
Term definitions and operational significance for maintainable policies.
Table
Groups chains and sets by address family, e.g. inet for both IPv4 and IPv6.
Chain
Processing points with hook and priority that determine when rules run.
Rule
A match and action pair, for example match tcp dport 22 then accept.
Example
sudo nft add table inet filter
sudo nft add chain inet filter input { type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop; }
sudo nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport 22 accept
Key Takeaway

Structure rules by role: use inet to avoid duplicated IPv4/IPv6 policies and place hooks logically for packet flow control.

Common misconceptions
  • inet does not convert payloads; it only unifies address-family configuration.
  • A default accept policy with ad-hoc drop rules is error-prone; prefer a default drop with explicit accepts for production hosts.
  • Hook priority matters when multiple tables interact with NAT and filtering.
Reflection

When you design policies, ask whether rules belong to the same logical table and whether using a single inet table reduces duplication while keeping intent clear.

screens.title: Sets and maps: grouping and mapping for concise rules
screens.subtitle: Use sets to group addresses and maps to associate values for dynamic policies

narration.text: Sets and maps are powerful features that reduce rule count and improve lookup performance. A set is a named collection of values, such as IP addresses or ports, that a rule can reference with a single match. For example, define a trusted internal IP set and accept traffic from that set on a management port. A map matches an input to a return value, letting you map a source address to a custom port number or label for downstream logic. In practice, use sets when multiple items share the same action, and use maps when a match must produce a variable outcome. Concrete example: create a set called trusted_internal_ips containing 192.168.50.0/24, then add a rule to accept tcp dport 8080 when the source address is in that set. A common mistake is using many duplicate accept rules instead of a single set reference—this increases maintenance burden and slows rule evaluation. Also consider the 'flags interval' option when adding ranges for space-efficient storage. Key takeaway: prefer sets and maps to express intent clearly and to scale policy management across dozens or hundreds of addresses.

keyIdea.title: Process
keyIdea.text: Create sets for shared matches and maps for value lookups to simplify and accelerate rule evaluation.

content.html:
Core › Sets & Maps
Process: Create and use sets

Steps to define a set, add elements, and reference it in a rule.

1. Declare a set
Use the correct family and type, e.g. type ipv4_addr for IPv4 subnets.
2. Add elements
Add multiple addresses together instead of repeating rules.
3. Reference in rules
Use @set_name syntax to match addresses in rules.
Example commands
sudo nft add set inet filter trusted_internal_ips { type ipv4_addr; flags interval; }
sudo nft add element inet filter trusted_internal_ips { 192.168.50.0/24 }
sudo nft add rule inet filter input ip saddr @trusted_internal_ips tcp dport 8080 accept
Key Takeaway

Use sets to centralize address lists and maps when matches must yield values, improving clarity and performance.

Maps: match to value

Maps let you translate a match into a returned value for dynamic policy behavior.

Analogy
Think of a set as a membership list and a map as a dictionary that returns a concrete action based on the lookup key.
Common mistake

Hardcoding many similar rules instead of centralizing values into a set makes audits and updates error-prone. Always consider whether a set or map simplifies maintenance.

screens.title: Connection tracking and stateful filtering
screens.subtitle: How ct state established,related enables safe session continuity

narration.text: Connection tracking is the mechanism that lets a firewall understand packet sequences as sessions rather than isolated datagrams. nftables exposes that functionality through the ct expression, allowing rules to match states such as established, related, and new. By accepting established and related packets you permit replies to previously allowed connections without creating overly permissive rules for incoming traffic. For example, after allowing outbound connections you should accept ct state established,related in the input chain so returning traffic is permitted. A concrete scenario: a web server accepts incoming HTTP; the connection tracker marks the session and subsequent packets belonging to that connection are allowed as established. A common misconception is to allow established traffic but forget to explicitly manage invalid state packets; include a rule to drop ct state invalid to reduce risk from malformed or spoofed packets. Also remember that connection tracking state interacts with NAT; DNAT may change destination addresses and the kernel will track that translated flow. Key takeaway: use stateful matches to keep rules concise and safe, but explicitly handle invalid states to reduce attack surface and unexpected behavior.

keyIdea.title: Connection tracking
keyIdea.text: Stateful matches let you accept replies and related traffic while keeping initial acceptance rules narrow.

content.html:
Definition › Connection tracking
What is connection tracking?

A kernel facility that classifies packets as new, established, related, or invalid so the firewall can apply stateful rules.

Rule example
sudo nft add rule inet filter input ct state established,related accept
Best practice
  • Allow established and related to enable replies without opening new inbound ports.
  • Drop invalid state packets explicitly to reduce malformed traffic risks.
Concrete scenario

A client connects to your server's HTTPS port. The server replies. The connection tracker marks both directions as part of the same session, allowing the server's replies to be accepted if established is permitted.

Common mistake
Relying only on broad accept rules for replies instead of using ct state can allow unexpected inbound sessions. Be explicit.
Key Takeaway

Use connection tracking to keep stateful policies concise; always handle invalid state packets explicitly.

screens.title: NAT basics: prerouting vs postrouting, DNAT and SNAT
screens.subtitle: Where to place NAT rules and why hook order matters

narration.text: Network Address Translation changes packet IP addresses to remap traffic between networks. The two common operations are Destination NAT, which changes the destination address or port for incoming traffic, and Source NAT, which changes the source address for outgoing traffic. In nftables, DNAT belongs in the prerouting hook because the destination must be altered before routing decisions. SNAT or masquerade belongs in postrouting, after the kernel determines the outgoing interface. A concrete example: to forward external port 8081 to an internal host at 192.168.1.10:80, you add a DNAT rule in the ip nat table prerouting chain that matches iifname "eth0" and tcp dport 8081, then dnat to the internal address. For outgoing masquerade, add a postrouting rule that matches oifname "eth0" and applies masquerade. A common misconception is treating NAT and forwarding as independent of enabling kernel forwarding; forgetting to enable net. ipv4. ip_forward will stop forwarded packets even if NAT rules are correct. Key takeaway: place DNAT in prerouting, SNAT in postrouting, enable IP forwarding when acting as a gateway, and verify with nft list ruleset and live tests.

keyIdea.title: Comparison
keyIdea.text: DNAT in prerouting changes destinations before routing; SNAT/masquerade in postrouting alters sources after routing decisions.

content.html:
NAT › DNAT vs SNAT
Destination NAT (DNAT)

Change destination address/port of incoming packets before routing decisions using prerouting.

sudo nft add table ip nat
sudo nft add chain ip nat prerouting { type nat hook prerouting priority -100; }
sudo nft add rule ip nat prerouting iifname "eth0" tcp dport 8081 dnat to 192.168.1.10:80
Why prerouting?
Packets must have their destination rewritten before the kernel decides where to route them, so the routing decision directs them to the correct internal host.
Source NAT (SNAT / Masquerade)

Change source addresses for outgoing packets after routing decisions using postrouting, commonly for masquerading internal networks.

sudo nft add chain ip nat postrouting { type nat hook postrouting priority 100; }
sudo nft add rule ip nat postrouting oifname "eth0" masquerade
Common mistake
Forgetting to enable IP forwarding in the kernel (net.ipv4.ip_forward) will prevent forwarded flows even if NAT rules appear correct.
Key Takeaway

DNAT belongs in prerouting; SNAT and masquerade belong in postrouting. Always enable and verify IP forwarding when forwarding packets between interfaces.

screens.title: Safe testing and rollback patterns
screens.subtitle: How to change firewall state without locking yourself out

narration.text: When updating firewall rules on a remotely managed server, preventing accidental lockout is essential. A reliable pattern is to schedule an automatic rollback before applying the change. For example, set an at job that flushes the ruleset in five minutes unless you cancel it after verifying connectivity. Alternatively, work from a maintenance console or a separate out-of-band management path. The hands-on commands in the chapter show a safe sequence: stop unwanted firewalld services, install and enable nftables, flush existing rules, define the inet table and chains with a default drop for input, then add accept rules. After adding rules, test SSH, HTTP, and other services immediately. If anything breaks, the scheduled flush will restore access. Another practical tip is to use tmux or screen so your session survives disconnects. A common misconception is that saving the rules immediately prevents recovery; if you save a broken ruleset and enable a service that loads it on boot, you may need console access to fix it. Key takeaway: always plan a rollback or use a safe test window when changing firewall policies, and validate services before persisting the ruleset to disk.

keyIdea.title: Process
keyIdea.text: Schedule a timed rollback or use a console to test new firewall rules before persisting to avoid lockout.

content.html:
Hands-on › Safe testing
Safe rollout steps
  1. Open a persistent console session with tmux or screen.
  2. Schedule a rollback: echo "nft flush ruleset" | at now + 5 minutes.
  3. Apply your nft changes and test connectivity quickly.
  4. Cancel the rollback when verified and persist the ruleset to /etc/nftables.conf.
Example rollback command
echo "nft flush ruleset" | at now + 5 minutes
Common pitfall

Persisting a broken ruleset immediately can prevent remote recovery. Verify first, then save.

Verification checklist
  • Can you SSH in from an external IP?
  • Are HTTP and HTTPS reachable from a browser or curl test?
  • Can a machine in the trusted subnet reach management ports?
  • Does port forwarding reach the internal service?
If a test fails, rely on the rollback or the console to restore access, then iterate on the ruleset. Only persist when tests pass.

screens.title: iptables basics and migration strategies
screens.subtitle: When to translate rules and when to re-architect in nftables

narration.text: iptables remains present in many environments, especially older distributions or appliances. It organizes rules into tables such as filter, nat, mangle, and raw, with separate binaries for IPv4 and IPv6. The translation path to nftables can use a utility that translates iptables-save output into an nft equivalent, which is handy for inspection and short migrations. However, translated rules may replicate legacy patterns that fail to leverage sets, maps, or the inet family. A better approach in many cases is to re-architect the policy in nftables: consolidate duplicated IPv4/IPv6 rules into inet tables, replace repeated address lists with sets, and translate per-flow matches to map-driven logic if needed. Concrete example: an iptables rule like iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT becomes an nftables rule in the inet filter input chain matching tcp dport 22 accept. A common misconception is that automated translation is always sufficient; it can produce correct behavior but often keeps inefficiencies. Key takeaway: use translation tools to learn and validate, but prefer re-architecting to gain the benefits of nftables features and maintainability. iptables basics and migration strategies means use translation tools to inspect legacy policies, but re-architect rulesets to exploit nftables' sets, maps, and inet family for cleaner, faster policies.. In practical terms, when to translate rules and when to re-architect in nftables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Architecture
keyIdea.text: Use translation tools to inspect legacy policies, but re-architect rulesets to exploit nftables' sets, maps, and inet family for cleaner, faster policies.

content.html:
Legacy › iptables & migration
iptables snapshot

Separate commands for IPv4 and IPv6, organized by tables and chains.

iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
When migrating, first capture iptables rules, run a translation utility to see the nftables equivalent, and then decide whether to import or redesign for clarity and performance.
Migration guidance
  • Use iptables-restore-translate to inspect conversions.
  • Prefer re-architecting rather than one-to-one translation to exploit sets and inet.
  • Test translated rules in a staging environment before production rollout.
Key Takeaway

Translate for quick inspection, but re-architect in nftables to reduce duplication and leverage modern features.

screens.title: DoS mitigation and rate limiting
screens.subtitle: Use nftables limit expressions to slow brute-force and flood attempts

narration.text: Firewalls contribute to Denial of Service mitigation by limiting rates, blocking known bad ranges, and dropping invalid packets early. nftables provides a limit qualifier that allows rules to accept traffic at a specified rate and burst, which is useful to slow brute-force or simple flood attacks. For example, an HTTP rule with a limit of 10 per second and a burst of 20 can drop excessive new connections while allowing normal traffic. For SSH brute-force protection, a lower rate such as 5 per minute with a modest burst reduces credential guessing attempts without blocking legitimate admins who occasionally reconnect. A concrete rule: add a rule in the inet filter input chain matching tcp dport 22 limit rate 5/minute burst 10 packets accept. A common mistake is applying a rate limit universally to an already-busy service, which can deny legitimate high-volume clients; instead, apply rate limits selectively or combine them with monitoring and known-good IP lists in sets. Key takeaway: rate limiting is a blunt but effective tool—tune rates carefully, pair with trusted IP sets, and monitor impact on legitimate users.

keyIdea.title: Mitigation
keyIdea.text: Rate limits reduce attack surface for floods and brute-force attempts; tune rates and combine with trusted sets for accuracy.

content.html:
Security › DoS Mitigation
Rate limiting pattern

Apply limits to specific service ports to throttle abusive connection rates while preserving legitimate traffic.

Example rule for SSH
sudo nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport 22 limit rate 5/minute burst 10 packets accept
Tuning tips
  • Measure baseline traffic before choosing a rate.
  • Apply limits per-IP where possible to avoid global throttles.
  • Combine with trusted IP sets to exempt known administrators.
Monitoring

Log dropped or limited packets and watch for legitimate clients being affected. Rate limiting should be part of a layered defense with network and application controls.

Key Takeaway

Use selective rate limits to slow attacks without degrading normal traffic; pair with trusted sets and monitoring for best results.

screens.title: Web server scenario — end-to-end configuration
screens.subtitle: Build the ruleset that secures a web server and performs port forwarding

narration.text: Apply what you've learned with a practical scenario: secure a web server that must accept SSH, HTTP, and HTTPS; allow all outgoing connections; block other incoming traffic; rate-limit SSH; permit management port 8080 from a trusted internal subnet; and forward external port 8081 to an internal host. The chapter provides a ready sequence: flush existing rules, create an inet filter table with input and output chains, accept established and related connections, allow the three service ports, add a SSH rate-limit rule, define a trusted_internal_ips set and allow tcp dport 8080 from that set, then create an ip nat table prerouting chain and add a DNAT rule matching iifname eth0 tcp dport 8081 to the internal address. Remember to enable ip_forward and add a postrouting masquerade rule if internal hosts need outbound NAT. Test each service from appropriate networks, and only persist the rules to /etc/nftables. conf when you're satisfied. A common misconception is to rely on interface names becoming stable; verify interface names like eth0/eth1 in your environment before applying NAT rules. Key takeaway: follow the test-then-persist workflow and verify connectivity for each rule you add.

keyIdea.title: Scenario
keyIdea.text: Implement a default-drop inet ruleset, allow required services, rate-limit SSH, create trusted IP sets, and perform DNAT for port forwarding.

content.html:
Lab › Web server scenario
Starter commands
sudo nft flush ruleset
sudo nft add table inet filter
sudo nft add chain inet filter input { type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop; }
sudo nft add chain inet filter forward { type filter hook forward priority 0; policy drop; }
sudo nft add chain inet filter output { type filter hook output priority 0; policy accept; }
sudo nft add rule inet filter input ct state established,related accept
sudo nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport { 22, 80, 443 } accept
sudo nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport 22 limit rate 5/minute burst 10 packets accept
Trusted set and NAT
sudo nft add set inet filter trusted_internal_ips { type ipv4_addr; flags interval; }
sudo nft add element inet filter trusted_internal_ips { 192.168.50.0/24 }
sudo nft add rule inet filter input ip saddr @trusted_internal_ips tcp dport 8080 accept

sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
sudo nft add table ip nat
sudo nft add chain ip nat prerouting { type nat hook prerouting priority -100; }
sudo nft add chain ip nat postrouting { type nat hook postrouting priority 100; }
sudo nft add rule ip nat prerouting iifname "eth0" tcp dport 8081 dnat to 192.168.1.10:80
sudo nft add rule ip nat postrouting oifname "eth0" masquerade
Key Takeaway

Follow the test-then-persist workflow, verify interface names and forwarding, and only save /etc/nftables.conf after successful verification.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Remember these compact ideas as you operate Linux firewalls. First, nftables uses tables, chains, and rules; prefer the inet family to avoid separate IPv4 and IPv6 configurations. Second, sets and maps are your friends for grouping addresses and mapping matches to values—use them to simplify and speed up rule evaluation. Third, NAT must be placed in the correct hooks: use prerouting for DNAT and postrouting for SNAT or masquerade, and always enable IP forwarding when acting as a gateway. These concepts form the foundation of resilient, maintainable firewall policies. Keep them in mind when you test, migrate, or persist configurations so your servers remain reachable and secure. narration.text: Keep three practical checks in mind: one, verify interface names and IP forwarding before applying NAT rules so forwarding works as expected. Two, prefer sets and maps to reduce duplicated rules and lower maintenance overhead; this also reduces the chance of subtle errors when ranges change. Three, always test rules with a rollback mechanism or console access; if you must persist a ruleset, only do so after a successful verification sequence. These checks are quick but prevent the most common operational mistakes when working with nftables and iptables. Checklist › Practical Checks
Interface & Forwarding
Confirm names like eth0/eth1 and enable net.ipv4.ip_forward when NAT is used.
Centralize lists
Use sets to manage trusted IPs and avoid repeating similar rules.
Safe deployment
Schedule rollbacks, use a console, and verify services before saving rules permanently.
Final thought
Small checks prevent major outages. Make them part of every firewall change workflow.
